title: Which steps are friction and which are thinking
description: Every step a product removes from a journey is a step where the user used to verify something. Nobody is accounting for what happens when all of them are gone. Product design has treated step reduction as an unqualified good since the first checkout funnels. Fewer clicks, fewer fields, fewer screens between question and answer. Intercom put it cleanly in 2021: the only purpose of a product is to help someone go from A to B, and the fewer steps, the better the journey . That rule still stands while the steps you remove are friction. But it breaks when the step you remove is where people are doing the thinking. Searching used to mean typing keywords, scanning ten links, picking one that looked credible, reading it, deciding whether to believe it, and checking a second source. Growth.design lists that sequence as the problem AI chat solves. Picking, believing, checking. But half that sequence is the user evaluating a claim. Removing those steps transfers a job from the reader to the engine. Which steps in your flow are overhead, and which ones are someone deciding something? Most teams have never separated the two. Ask what happens between two steps Take any two screens in your product and ask what sits between them. Not what the user clicks. What the user has to work out on their own. Does the person have to guess something the interface never told them? What are they deciding, and did you give them anything to decide with? The gaps hide in the seconds after an action, when the product goes quiet. Someone clicks “Start free trial” and lands on a dashboard with no indication of what the trial covers, when it ends, or what to do first. Nothing broke. The flow works. But the person is still guessing. Samuel Hulick made this the center of his article in Mind the Gap , and it remains one of the fastest audit in product design because it costs nothing. Open your own signup flow and write down every moment you had to know something the screen did not say. Feedforward is the principle underneath: showing what will happen next before someone acts. A user hovering over “Submit” with no idea whether that clears the form, sends an email, or charges a card is standing in a gap you left. The cues that close it are small enough that nobody thanks you for them. The journey starts before your product and ends after it Someone did not wake up wanting to use your app. They wanted to book a flight or get information about which SUV to buy. Your product intersects a path that started somewhere else and continues after they close the tab. Map that longer path and two things become visible: where each step could carry less weight, and where you have inserted your own priorities into someone else’s route. The email capture before the content. The plan selector before the person knows what the plans do. The product tour that starts before anyone has used the product. Timing is the whole argument. A phone number field reads as routine at checkout and as a toll on a landing page. Same request, different moment, opposite outcomes. There is a time and place for the business ask, and it is later than most teams put it. The peak-end rule is worth understanding here. People judge an experience by its most intense moment and its ending, not by an average of the steps. A journey with one excellent moment and a clean finish beats a smooth one nobody remembers. Map for the peak and the end, then spend your effort there. Every element on the screen is serving someone Open most apps and something wants to sell you before you have done anything. Go back to the reason the person came. Take a screen and go element by element. Why is this person here? What are they trying to finish? Does this element serve that, or does it serve a metric on your dashboard? The distinction between those last two is the work. A “Refer a friend” banner on an empty-state dashboard serves the growth target. A “Refer a friend” prompt after someone completes their third successful project serves both. Same component, different placement, and only one of them is honest about the moment it sits in. Hick’s law gives you the cost of getting this wrong. Response time grows with each option added, and a checkout with six payment options, three shipping tiers, and a promo field visible at once stalls people who arrived ready to buy. Cutting choices is not the same as cutting complexity. The goal is fewer decisions at any one moment, not a product that decides for people. Group what belongs together, then space out the rest Most redesigns start here. Everything sits at the same visual weight, related things drift apart, and the screen offers no structure to read. Put related elements close. Push unrelated ones apart. Let the interface breathe. It sounds too basic to write down, and it accounts for more redesign work than any sophisticated technique. Proximity is doing the work. Place two things near each other and people assume they are related, whether or not you meant them to be. Grouping is meaning. That assumption works for you or against you depending on how carefully you place things, which is why a “Cancel subscription” link sitting eight pixels from “Update payment method” produces support tickets. Spacing is the other half and gets cut first when a screen fills up. Space is what makes a group readable as a group. The content decides the container Design without content is coloring. The design of a page depends on what goes inside it. Start with a menu or a box and you are arranging containers for text nobody has written, which means the text will later be trimmed to fit the box. The box wins. It should not. Start with the job instead. What is this person trying to get done, and what do they need in front of them to do it? Real content, real length, real edge cases. The longest product name. The empty state. The error. Jesse James Garrett put content underneath structure in his five planes model . Skeleton and surface sit on top of scope and structure. Designing the surface before the scope exists inverts the model, and every designer who has placed lorem ipsum into a product knows how that ends. What AI search does to all five AI chat collapses the search journey. Type a question, get an answer, refine with a chip labeled “best budget” or “fuel efficiency,” decide. Twenty seconds, no source opened. By every measure in this article, that is a better journey. Fewer steps. Less friction. The person got from A to B. The refinement chips are the part to look at closely. Tapping through them feels like exploring. The person is choosing among options the engine wrote, narrowing inside a frame they did not set. The frame came with the answer. If people stop exploring, publishers lose the traffic that funds the writing the engine summarizes. The engine’s quality rests on a supply it is defunding. Neither Microsoft nor Google has explained how that resolves. The design lesson is narrower than the media one. When you remove a step that contained thinking and decision making, you owe the person a way back into it. Authority bias explains why: fluent, confident, well-formatted output reads as verified, and the interface never signals otherwise. I wrote about the presentation side of this in when tools pretend to be people . This is the structural side. A system can drop every human affectation and still remove your verification steps by collapsing the journey. Removing steps is usually right. Know which ones. — Thanks for reading. The newsletter stays free, and I’d like to keep it that way. Your support makes that possible. Psychology of Design Four of the five tactics above run on principles I’ve spent years documenting. Feedforward, Hick’s law, proximity, peak-end. I keep the whole set in one place. 106 principles, each written as a working tool. What it is, how it shows up in real interfaces, where to apply it, and the companies already using it. A searchable Notion database you keep open while you work: filter by cluster, find the principle that fits the screen in front of you, ship something that fits how people are wired. From the Zeigarnik Effect to the Labor Illusion to Hick’s Law. Get the 106 principles →

title: Taste at scale
description: The agency model was always a headcount problem. More clients meant more people. Margins stayed thin because the work couldn’t scale faster than the team. Every studio I watched operate ran into the same ceiling: the work was good, the growth was slow, and the business was fragile. I built Nirmata to see whether one person with the right tools and judgment could do what used to require a team of eight. The answer is yes. With a few things worth saying out loud. The economics changed Software used to be expensive to build . Three things collapsed at roughly the same time: the cost of execution, the cost of coordination, and the cost of custom software. When those three things were expensive, you needed specialists for each, and a project manager to stitch them together. When they got cheap, the specialists became overhead. AI writing code is the obvious story. The less obvious one is what that does to project economics. . A custom interface that used to require two weeks of a senior developer’s time can come together in days. A design system that would have needed a dedicated sprint now gets built alongside the thing it governs. The friction between design and development, the handoff cost that every agency has tried and failed to eliminate, shrinks to almost nothing when one person is handling both ends with AI in the loop. That’s the mechanical case for Nirmata. Design and development as a single continuous process, owned by one studio, delivered at a pace the traditional model structurally can’t match. Where product work actually breaks Most product work fails at the boundary between disciplines. The designer doesn’t understand what’s expensive to build. The developer doesn’t know which edge cases the design was trying to solve. The PM is translating between them and losing signal in both directions. By the time something ships, it’s a negotiated object, shaped more by coordination cost than by the original intent. Whoever can hold design, engineering, and product decisions in the same head and act on all three without waiting for a meeting will outshine a committee every time. What gets cheaper is execution. What stays expensive is knowing what to build, why it matters, and whether the thing you shipped is actually working. Coding agents accelerate shipping, which puts pressure on the part that teams have always struggled with most. That part has stayed stubbornly manual, even as everything around it gets automated. A ticket manager who creates tasks and tracks status is overhead in this model. Judgment isn’t. A studio that controls the full cycle removes most of the translation steps. The thinking that shapes the design is the same thinking that decides how it gets built. That continuity shows up in the work. What the freed space is for The design founder era is partly about aesthetics and partly about this. Founders who can hold the visual and the technical in the same head reliably build things that feel coherent. The interface and the system underneath it are solving the same problem, in the same register. When agents handle the implementation, something shifts. The cognitive overhead of writing code drops out, and the mental space it occupied goes somewhere else. For me, it goes toward the psychology of what gets built. Why does this pattern create anxiety? Why does this flow cause people to abandon? What does this decision cost the user versus what it earns the product? I’ve spent years building a library of over a hundred psychological principles that apply directly to product decisions, documented at 1984.design . Loss aversion, cognitive load, the peak-end rule, decision fatigue. Applied directly, they separate a feature that serves users from one that extracts from them. Dark patterns (aka deceptive patterns ) exist because most builders never slow down enough to ask whether what they’re shipping is actually good for the person on the other end. Coding with agents creates that space. The speed is a side effect. The more important thing is what you can think about while the code gets written. The caution YC’s Spring 2026 request list named it: AI-native agencies running at software-level margins, same output, none of the coordination cost. A model that treats headcount as a variable, not a fixed input. Nirmata was built on that assumption before the framing existed. AI-written code still needs someone accountable for what it does. Security, reliability, IP, those don’t disappear because the code came fast. I treat oversight as part of the work, not something you add at the end. What remains AI absorbed the execution layer. What’s left is editorial work: knowing what to build, recognizing when it’s right, deciding when to stop. The design bar will keep rising alongside this. Builders who ship more can iterate faster, which means the gap between good taste and no taste compounds over time. AI also improves its own design output , so even companies for whom design wasn’t a priority will get access to better defaults. The premium moves entirely to taste, the ability to recognize what works, what doesn’t, and why. A one-person studio doing the full cycle lives in that space. Which problems are worth solving. Which tradeoffs to accept. How to hold a coherent vision from the first conversation to the thing that ships. AI handles the rest. That’s why I’m building Nirmata . Thanks for reading. — B.

title: Diana Kellogg updates her Tribeca home using salvaged materials
description: New York architect Diana Kellogg has renovated her historic Tribeca residence, highlighting materials repurposed from its industrial past. Kellogg and her family have occupied the home on Staple Street for 25 years, which is close to the studio that the architect shares with her filmmaker husband. Diana Kellogg has updated her home gradually over time, while retaining its industrial character The building originally served as cold storage for neighbouring produce distribution facilities, then became a plumber's supply storefront and eventually a residence around 50 years ago. Kellogg has renovated and updated the structure gradually over the years, and when her kids moved out, she decided to undertake a more comprehensive overhaul. Many of the built-in elements are formed from the salvage of the building's freight elevator An old freight elevator was removed and replaced with a space that Kellogg refers to as the Green Room. The glass-wrapped nook is lined with cushioned seating and used for intimate catch-ups over drinks, or private video calls. The kitchen similarly utilises salvaged elements The salvage from the elevator and other elements around the building were repurposed to create structures for the kitchen, bookcases, and a staircase that connects the four levels. "Throughout the house there were old glass and steel doors, and windows and stuff," Kellogg said. "I just moved them around and repurposed them." A space dubbed the Green Room is used for catch-ups and Zoom calls In keeping with the architecture, the decor remains industrial and spare, highlighting key elements like the fireplace and the 25-foot-long chestnut beams that span the ceiling. "It was a massive pain in the neck to strip those, but one of the best decisions we made, because they add so much warmth and character," said Kellogg. A steel staircase connects the home's four levels During the most recent renovation, the upstairs bedrooms with vaulted brick ceilings were reconfigured as neutrally decorated spaces separated by sliding mahogany doors. On the ground floor, the children's former playroom – complete with climbing ropes and a swing – was converted into a comfortable TV room, featuring a large L-shaped sofa and a variety of midcentury furniture pieces. The ground-floor children's playroom was recently converted into a media room Matching those on the level above, Noguchi pendant lights hang from the steel beams that Kellogg added to suspend the "jungle gym". "There's still one climbing rope down there that people think is an art piece, which I love," she said. Read: Crina Arghirescu Rogard adds "eccentric design" to historic penthouse in Tribeca Key artworks include a pair of photographs by Ljubodrag Andric , which he produced to sit either side of the first-floor fireplace and "give the place so much depth and warmth," said Kellogg. Downstairs, the walls are adorned with images of The Rajkumari Ratnavati Girl's School that Kellogg completed in 2021 in India's Thar Desert. Upstairs bedrooms are divided by mahogany sliding doors The roof terrace was relandscaped with planters and a variety of wooden outdoor furniture that forms dining and seating areas with views of a historic bridge between the adjacent buildings. "I really wanted an oasis up there, and to have it be a second living room," said Kellogg. "And there's the fabulous bridge, which we have kind of great views of from our house – which is, in my opinion, better than actually being inside it." The roof terrace was also refurbished with planters and outdoor furniture Many of Tribeca's former industrial buildings are now residential, housing large lofts and penthouses, while others contain galleries and creative spaces. Examples of other homes in the neighbourhood include a penthouse in the American Thread Building updated by Crina Arghirescu Rogard and a loft that Andrea Leung renovated to conceal "secret spaces". The photography is by Andrew Brinka . The post Diana Kellogg updates her Tribeca home using salvaged materials appeared first on Dezeen .

title: The two forces that help build opportunity
description: Hey pals, I hope all is good in your world. Today we are going to dive a little deeper into two very important elements that build recognisable reputations and brands… and why I built the Opportunity Design Course + Course Club (Early Bird enrollment closes this Sunday!). The two elements? Perception & Evidence. Firstly I want to explain what these two things are individually. Evidence: This is what you’ve actually done. It’s the real, tangible proof of your work. The products you’ve built, the testimonials you’ve earned from your clients, the projects you’ve delivered to your people, the impact you’ve created as a whole. It’s the truth, the receipts, the stuff that stands up in a court of freaking law. Perception: This is what people think you’ve done. It’s how your brand is experienced from the outside. It’s the story that forms in someone’s head long before they ever meet you, talk to you, or work with you. Simply put... Evidence = what is true and provable. Perception = what people believe to be true based on what they can see. The big old problem we all have as creative humans, especially those who have been in the game for a fair chunk of time... it’s impossible for anyone to have access to ALL of your evidence. Most people won’t see the hours you’ve poured in a project, the thinking behind your decisions, or how much bloody effort goes into what you do every damn day. They often just see the end result and that’s where their opinion forms. That’s why perception, in many cases, outweighs evidence... and why perception is super important in brand building. You could be absolutely brilliant at what you do, but if nobody knows it, it doesn’t exist in their world. You might have the work to back it up, but if the way you show up looks sloppy or inconsistent... or you do not show up at all... people will think twice and find another option. That doesn’t mean perception is about pretending or faking it for the internet or your clients in general. It’s about making it easier for people to find the truth, and to do that, you need to give them access to your evidence. Our job as humans who own businesses is to make sure the perception of us from the outside aligns with the truth as closely as possible. Trust doesn’t come from either perception or evidence on its own… it grows when the two work together, and as you can see from the image below, that’s when you become a Power Brand. I personally believe we are all striving to become the “Power Brand” where our perception and evidence are high and in alignment, and the gap between them is very small. This is where true value is created and we become a much safer commercial choice for our clients. Opportunity happens consistently when the truth and perceived reality are best mates, standing together. Here is a little breakdown of each quadrant so you can understand where you might sit. High perception, high evidence: The Power Brand. People notice you and consistently experience the quality behind the perception. Your reputation matches the reality of what you actually deliver, which creates trust, momentum, and long-term opportunity. Every great brand we know masters this balance between perception and evidence. High perception, low evidence: The Hype Brand. You know how to grab attention and create excitement, but the reality underneath hasn’t fully caught up yet. Things can look bigger, stronger, or more established from the outside than they actually are once people get closer. Low perception, high evidence: The Hidden Genius Brand. You’re doing brilliant work, but not enough people currently get the chance to experience it. The skill, care, and trustworthiness are already there… your reputation just hasn’t spread far beyond your existing network yet. (I built Opportunity Design for you my friends) Low perception, low evidence: The Work-in-Progress Brand. You’re still figuring things out, experimenting, learning, and discovering where your strengths actually live. And honestly? That’s completely normal. Every powerful brand, business, and creative human starts as a work in progress. The big takeaway here? Branding isn’t just about reality... it’s also about perceived reality. People can’t choose you based on the evidence they have never seen. They can only choose you based on what they know, and ultimately, believe to be true about you. This is why I am so excited about The Opportunity Design Course + Course Club that starts next week. This is a 6-week programme designed to help you close the gap between what you’re capable of and what other people know you’re capable of, in order to create more extraordinary opportunities. I designed this for the Hidden Geniuses who need their perception to catch up with their evidence on their way to becoming a Power Brand. Inside the course, I share with you how I have intentionally created opportunities over the last few years with a super simple (but takes effort) system for building your perception up to align with all your existing evidence. I will show you how to prove you are valuable to the right people before they see value in you themselves. I will show you my frameworks to build commercial relationships that increase the probability of you being chosen. Here’s everything included: 12 pre-recorded lessons covering the Opportunity Design system. Six weeks of live group coaching, with a 90-minute call each week on Wednesdays. Our first call is Wednesday, 14th October. A private community space to stay connected, share what you’re learning, ask questions, and cheer each other on. That call is time to focus on your situation and the work you want, the people you want to reach, and how you can help them see more of what you’re capable of. If you’ve ever wanted to chat with me 1:1, this is your chance my friends. The programme starts with live calls every Wednesday starting on the 14th October . Join before 11th October to get the discount and your one-to-one call. JOIN THE OPPORTUNITY DESIGN COURSE CLUB No hacks, no shortcuts my friends. description: My friends, Over 20+ years in the creative industry, I’ve seen (and weathered) a lot of its ups and downs… new tech, social media, changing economies… These days, the creative industry is shifting big again, and the people feeling it most are the ones just starting out. Which, let’s be honest, is pretty shit. Students, juniors, early-stage creatives… you’re not just being squeezed financially, you’re carrying the mental side of it too. You’re constantly being told you’re replaceable. That AI is coming for your job. That the thing you’ve spent years learning might not matter anymore. And after a while, that kind of noise starts to play gams with the old brain. But, a lot of this noise is lazy thinking at best, because there is no future creative industry without creative people. And a world without creatives is not a world I, or anyone I speak to, wants to see. So… instead of just talking about it, I’ve teamed up with my awesome pals at Affinity to actually do something about it. The Affinity team is full of wonderful humans, and we share many of the same values and goals when it comes to making the world a better place and helping creative people from all walks of life succeed. So here we are… INTRODUCING THE SUPER DUPER® MENTORSHIP PROGRAM, sponsored by Affinity. The Super Duper Mentorship is a free four-month program designed to help emerging creatives build confidence, momentum, and real career opportunities. (*For the Mentorship,“emerging” means 5 years or less in the industry. If you’re further along in your creative journey, stay tuned for another program I’ll be launching later this year.) The program is f-r-e-e. Properly free. Not watered-down, stripped-back, “you get half the experience” kind of free… it’s the real fucking deal. It doesn’t matter where you’re based, what creative discipline you’re part of, what software you use, or where you’re at with your skillset. We’re all about backing people who are willing to show up and take action. Each cohort of the Super Duper Mentorship will have 100 creatives in it. If you don’t get in the first time, there’ll be another intake, and another after that. We’ll keep this going every year, for as long as people have the energy to show up and participate. If you’re a designer, artist, illustrator, photographer, or just a generally creative human wanting to make cool shit… this has been built for you. Key Dates: Applications Open: today, 30th June 2026 Applications close: 14th July 2026 (you’ll hear back from us by the 24th of July) Doors open for Cohort 1: Monday 3rd August 2026 Weekly calls: Tuesdays, 6pm BST The Mentorship will run online inside the private Super Duper Circle community, hosted by myself and some very special guest appearances. APPLY HERE What the Mentorship Covers: The program runs in two phases. Phase One: Reframing and Rethinking The first 90 days, we’ll focus on mindset, clarity, and direction. You’ll work through the habits, assumptions, and overthinking patterns that often hold creatives back. You’ll explore: creative positioning pricing and boundaries reputation and trust building an offer around your skills We’ll help you move from confusion and hesitation to confidence and clarity. Phase Two: Action and Application The final 30 days of the mentorship are where things get practical. We are going to build something real together: We will create some cool artwork Pop it onto some cool product Send you the items for freebies You can sell them to make some monies. Everything in the Super Duper Mentorship is practical and built around participation. You’re not just taking in advice, you’re applying it and taking action. Testing ideas, getting feedback, and refining as you go. By the end of our four months together, you’ll go from being good at your craft to becoming a more employable and entrepreneurial creative who can build opportunities around your skills, have real (and meaningful) conversations with real people, and turn your ideas into something that actually works in the real world. Let’s fucking go. And if you know someone who’s early on in their creative journey, send this their way. A friend, a son or daughter, a colleague… anyone who needs a bit of direction and a proper shot. I need your help to get this in front of the right people. title: The Industry Swap Experiment
description: An amazingly random thing happened this last week. I found myself in Moab, Utah, with around 70 total strangers who now feel like my best friends. I was invited by my buddy Jason to speak at the first-ever Summer Camp hosted by his company, Rupt, for the promotional products industry. There were team colours, a healthy dose of friendly competition, prizes, adventures and learning sessions, all set against the incredible backdrop of the Colorado River and the red rock desert. It was fucking Magical. As a brand guy I often find myself around brand people whether thats agency owners, designers or people building things in the creative space but I have always loved to pop myself in the deep water of the unknowing. I know very little about this world. Like most people, I’ve interacted with the industry countless times as an end user. Whether that’s branded merch, company swag, event giveaways or promotional products arriving in the post… but I’ve never actually spent too much time inside the industry itself or with the people who make it all happen… so on paper, I had absolutely no business being there. But that’s exactly why I jumped at the chance to speak at this event. I love learning new things, and this room was packed with some of the biggest hitters in the game. People who have spent years building businesses and solving problems in a world I know jack shit about. It would have been easy to say no. The travel was long, the industry was unfamiliar but saying no to this opportunity was never really on the cards for me. I am getting older, and as that happens, the more I think one of the biggest mistakes we make is only learning from people who do the same thing as us. We all read the same design books, follow pretty much the same people, attend the same conferences and end up having the same conversations over and over again. This felt like the exact opposite of that… I’m gonna call it the ‘anti-echo chamber’ move. An opportunity to step outside my own little corner of the world and spend time with people who think differently and see things through a completely different lens. I had a feeling it would open my brain up in ways it hadn’t been before, and it absolutely did. Now, even though this space doesn’t live and breathe design in the same way mine does, it still lives in the world of branding. Most brand people spend their time on the fun stuff like the thinking, story, and execution side of design. We help make strategic decisions, build the identity, and create the funky punky assets. Then, more often than not, we release the work into the wild and hope it finds its way. What really hit home for me whilst spending time with this incredible group of humans is that this industry is actually much closer to mine than I first realised. They’re positioned at an incredibly important point in the journey… where the identity of a company meets real humans in the real world. They are a key part of what we do because they help bring businesses to life through experiences. And ultimately, that’s where ‘brand status’ is earned. As brand people, we’re in the game of pattern building and memory. We help businesses become recognisable. The promotional products industry helps those companies show up in the real world, creating physical touch-points and experiences that reinforce everything the business is trying to stand for. The biggest takeaway for me this week, apart from the fact that Moab might be one of the coolest places on the planet, is that every industry has its own wisdom. Every industry has people solving interesting problems and has a lot of knowledge to offer the general outsider who is keen to learn a new perspective. It’s easy to convince ourselves that all the answers live inside our own little bubble, but I’ve found over the years that many of the best ideas and implementations in my own business have come from looking outside of design. Whether that’s borrowing hospitality thinking and applying it to my design process, or building an identity of my own that fuses tattoo culture with skate-shop vibes, the things that have helped me stand out have not come from simply doing what everyone else was doing. One of the ideas I shared during my talk was Hotelling’s Law … the observation that competitors naturally drift towards sameness because it feels safer. Over time, everyone starts looking similar, sounding similar and offering similar things because nobody wants to stray too far from what appears to be working for others. The irony though is that the safest thing to do often becomes the riskiest thing to do. If everybody moves towards the middle, the middle becomes really freaking crowded. Which is why I’ve always been more interested in pushing at the edges… That’s where the interesting opportunities live. That’s why I think we should all spend a little more time making anti-echo chamber moves. Here are some ways you can do that: 1. Go to the event that isn’t built for you. 2. Read the book that nobody in your industry is talking about. 3. Spend time with people who challenge your assumptions. 4. Put yourself in rooms where you’re not the expert. Remember, my friends… curiosity is often where the magic lives. And if my week in the Utah desert taught me anything, it’s that sometimes the most valuable thing you can do isn’t go deeper into your own world… It’s to spend some time exploring somebody else’s. Big love and respect. James - The People’s Branding Mentor

title: Tiny moments that become a real brand.
description: Before we jump into this week’s article, reminder that my new book No Bullsh*t Branding is available for pre-order… and if you pre-order by the end of today (Sunday 31st May) you get a bonus freebie bundle, including the Book Club, the new MVB Course, limited edition MBJ merch, and digital downloads. Check it out here ! Thank you all so much for your support. Last weekend the weather was delicious. So delicious that myself, Kate and Rocco went to the beach for the day to hang with our friends (Jamie & Mel) and their little kiddos… it was one of those beautiful little days that will live long in the memory bank. We were down at West Wittering beach near Chichester. It’s this big, magical stretch of sand where, when the tide goes out, the beach becomes absolutely colossal. Perfect for kids because there’s endless space to run around and play… it becomes the worlds largest, sandy adventure space. Scattered across the beach are these little pools of warm water left behind by the retreating tide… tiny, stinky lakes full of seaweed, shells, wet sand and mess. Basically heaven for a little dude like Rocco. And he was more than happy exploring them completely alone while the rest of his friends sat further up the beach eating lunch and digging holes. He was so happy, so I wanted him to just ‘be’… so I stayed and watched. After maybe an hour of watching him play in the same giant puddle, I eventually wandered up to him and asked him to come back to “base camp” so we could put more suncream on, tag mummy back in and potentially allow me to eat some lunch. But he was having absolutely none of it. Everything I offered was ignored. Every negotiation tactic I’d learned in business was useless, and every attempt to reason with him about how the sun was really hot and he needed protecting from it was completely pointless. Eventually Kate, my wonderful wife, spotted my slow descent into parental defeat from afar and wandered over with all the supplies we needed. And at that point, I just accepted reality and decided to play the waiting game until he was ready to move on himself… I mean, the sun would go down eventually, I was sure of that, and I also now had a sandwich. But there was a lesson hiding inside all of this. When you have very little to negotiate with, the situation you are in becomes incredibly difficult to win… and this got me thinking about the very beginning of my own business journey. It was so difficult to find any money-making opportunities when I started because I had so little to negotiate with. No Leverage. I had no real portfolio, no website, no testimonials and, in absolute honesty… very little knowledge. I wouldn’t have hired me. As you know, for me, a brand is a recognisable reputation, and at that point I was neither recognised nor did I really have a reputation worth knowing… unless it was “having a good time down the pub” - I was real good at that. And this got me thinking about all the newbies entering the world right now. All the junior creatives trying to find work and carve out a place for themselves while also navigating challenges I never had to deal with. Things like social media pressure, constant comparison, AI, tech and the heavy, heavy, heavy psychological weight of feeling like you need to live your life so publicly online. Now, I’m not saying my era had it easy at all… every generation has its own struggles. But I do think it’s harder now than it was 20 years ago, mainly for the reasons I mentioned above. So I want to try an answer this question today. How do we build a business when, right at the beginning, we have nothing to be recognised for and no reputation backing us up? So… lets chat. Yes, you might not have the clients yet. You might not have the case studies, the swanky portfolio, the testimonials or the years of industry proof backing up your ambition. But what you do have is YOU. That matters far more than many people think. Because there are already so many things you are recognised for outside of your “business circles”. Your attitude, your energy, your humour, your kindness, your curiosity, your willingness to help, your ability to make people feel good around you, your ability to stay optimistic when everything feels difficult or half empty. What I’m trying to suggest here is that even if you do not yet have a recognisable reputation around your work, you already have years and years of building a recognisable reputation around your humanness and character, and that is a beautifully fun place to start… that becomes your negotiating power. One of the huge advantages early stage creatives have is that they are not yet boxed in by the “rules” of the industry. They are not trapped by client expectations or weighed down by years of process refinement and predictability. They still have “all the raws”… raw energy, raw enthusiasm and raw creativity to boot. In the beginning, it’s often your willingness to care about others and build relationships that sparks the most opportunity. Helping a mate out for freebies, offering your services to friends of friends in exchange for tickets to their latest gig… that scrappy little world of free crafty goodness is where most of us cut our teeth in the industry. When I was starting out, I bartered constantly. I used my skills to build experience, and the more experience I gained, the more confidence I built. In return, I’d get free coffee, free jewellery, free food, whilst also building relationships with local humans… whatever people could offer at the time instead of money, I said yes to. Looking back, I actually think there’s something incredibly beautiful about that stage of the journey. I mean, bartering is how worlds were built. When you’re starting out, you still have permission to try almost anything you can to keep the lights on and keep the dream alive. You can knock on doors, start conversations, help people, make things, experiment, build fabulous little ditties and push your creativity out into the world. And over time, people begin recognising you for those behaviours. For your energy, your effort, your generosity, your consistency and the way you make people feel. Almost without noticing it, those tiny moments become the foundations of a recognisable reputation. A real brand. So if you are at the beginning, listening to a noisy world telling you that “designers are fucked” or “the creative industry is doomed,” remember that most of it is just distraction… like a lot of news on the inter webs. Don’t fall into the trap of blindly listening to these people. Many of them have their own agenda too… which is often making sure they stay relevant and irreplaceable in a changing world. Instead, use your creativity and your energy to build relationships. Make cool stuff and send it to people. Write a little hand-drawn note thanking somebody for inspiring you. Instead of sending the same PDF portfolio to 400 people like everybody else is doing, start more real, human conversations. Barter your services. Collaborate with people. Send a hand written letter. Deliver someone a little product with your work on it. Go above and beyond simply because you care enough to do so. Become recognised for how much effort you are putting in… that is a reputation that opportunities will eventually flow towards. Stay Focused, Stay Crafty… Your creativity is your super duper power. James - The Peoples Branding Mentor

title: The Unscriptable Moments That Build Reputation
description: Hello my champions of creative goodness. How are ya? Today I want to dive into a little topic that I am super passionate about, and that is the human goodness we can do to elevate the experience for the people we work with. Everyone reading this is a craft-based, creativity-infused builder of things. You might own a business, work with brands, or create cool visuals for people who love looking at cool visuals. I don’t think creative people like that need motivation to continue doing the things they already do so well, but I do think there is another layer we often forget to think about… the human layer. The stuff on top of the craft. That is where some new magic can be found. It looks like over the coming years a lot of businesses and brands will automate huge parts of their customer journey, which is logical, so the question for me becomes… Where does the human come in and make a decision that was not obvious? I am all for becoming more efficient and dialling in a good process, as many of you will know, but it’s often the stupid-on-paper, “not good for business” decisions that build a reputation worth talking about. One of my favourite examples of human creativity elevating a brand’s reputation is the story of Joshie the Giraffe. A family went on holiday to California and accidentally left their son’s stuffed giraffe at a Ritz-Carlton hotel where they were staying. To put the little boy at ease, his dad told a little white lie and said Joshie had decided to stay behind for an extra holiday. The dad had phoned the hotel and asked if they could find it, send it back, and hopefully reunite the little guy with his giraffe. The hotel staff found Joshie amongst the laundry and could have simply posted the toy back. But instead, they created an entire photo album showing Joshie relaxing by the pool, driving golf carts, getting spa treatments with cucumbers over his eyes, and “enjoying his extended vacation” before finally sending him home, all to back up his dad’s story. That tiny, unscriptable moment of human creativity transformed a forgotten toy into a story that millions of people still talk about today… just like I am right now. And I think that’s freaking fascinating. Because I doubt that family remembers much about the facilities at the Ritz-Carlton, the weather, or even how good the food was… but they will absolutely remember Joshie’s holiday forever. This got the old curiosity up… Why do moments like this stick with us so deeply while so many other experiences disappear from memory almost immediately? Why do we instantly want to tell our mates about them, repost them online and emotionally connect with complete strangers because of them? For that we probably need to get a little ‘sciencey’. Now remember, I’m not a scientist. I’m just an inquisitive bloke with a scraggly beard who spends far too much time researching human behaviour, but here’s what I found out… Your brain is basically a very clever prediction machine. Most of the time, your brain is trying to conserve energy by guessing what is about to happen next based on previous experiences and familiar patterns. If things go exactly as expected, the brain doesn’t need to pay much attention because nothing new or important is happening. Win for brain power. This is why most of our routine experiences disappear from memory almost immediately. If you are anything like me, you get in the car, drive somewhere you’ve been a thousand times before, pull up, get out, and suddenly realise you barely even remember the journey itself. You obviously drove, stopped at traffic lights and avoided crashing into things, but because your brain already knew the pattern, most of the drive happened on complete autopilot… and it’s even easier now I don’t have to change gears anymore. Thank fook for the automatic. Humans do this constantly. We predict things, filter things and automate familiar experiences because if we had to consciously process every tiny detail of every moment of every day we would mentally collapse before our cheeky 11am coffee break. That’s why so many experiences we go through every single day become, well… forgettable. You expect the hotel room to be ready when you arrive. You expect somebody at reception to hand you a key, point you towards the lift or stairs and solve any mini problems in the quickest and most logical way possible, so when all of those things happen exactly as predicted, your brain simply processes the experience efficiently and moves on because nothing emotionally interesting actually happened. But when something interrupts that predictable pattern in a creative, emotional or unexpected way, your brain suddenly pays far more attention because it wasn’t expecting it. That’s why the Joshie story mattered so freaking much. The family expected the hotel to find the giraffe and simply post it back. Problem solved. No dramas here people. Everybody moves on with their lives. But instead, the hotel staff created this ridiculously brilliant, fake holiday for the giraffe that made it feel like Joshie was genuinely out there living his best life in the California sun and making mates along the way. They went to completely unreasonable measures just to bring a little bit of joy to a child and back up his dad’s white lie, and that exact unpredictability is what made the whole thing unforgettable. Humans remember meaningful and surprising moments far more than they remember predictable and functional ones. The hotel didn’t just solve the problem. They transformed a completely ordinary customer service interaction into a story that people are still retelling years later… and I think that’s the bit most of us miss as business owners. People rarely remember what was efficient, but they almost always remember how something made them feel. I mean, I almost bloody cried the first time I read the Joshie story because I instantly thought about how my own son would feel seeing his favourite toy off living its best life and making mates on holiday. I take Lightning McQueen with me on work trips because I miss my son Rocco, and I take silly little photos of him at random places because I know my son lights up when he sees them. He genuinely thinks daddy and Lightning are away together having a good time, so this little giraffe story hit a proper emotional note for me. The Joshie story stopped being “good customer service” and instantly became something far more human because you could feel the love, effort and humanity inside the decision those hotel staff made… and that kind of creativity can never be automated. Nor bloody should it. I hope this story sparks the creativity inside you to go against the grain when you can. To be unpredictable with your kindness and to find ways to connect with others that might be out of the ordinary. People remember people who thought about them in different and unique ways. I think, over the coming years, businesses and brands will increasingly be judged on what they choose to keep human. Automate the predictable. Humanise the meaningful. Love ya. James - The People’s Branding Mentor

title: What A Coincidence
description: * This was meant to go out yesterday, but there was a glitch on my end. Sorry! * Reminder: The Savor of the Month theme for September is STRIPES. Details here ; Supporters can share their findings in the thread here . So many great contributions! Check it out ! “ coincidence ,” by K Bahr on Flickr “A coincidence, after all, has to be noticed.“ Dear friend of TAoN Suzanne M sent me a link the other day to a deep-dive article about coincidences . I’d never given this subject much thought, but it turned out to be pretty interesting. And as Suzanne detected, there was a noticing/attention angle that I couldn’t help dwelling on. A coincidence, after all, has to be noticed. If I walk past a childhood friend I haven’t seen in 20 years in some airport where neither of us lives, one of us has to notice the other for the coincidence to “count,” as it were. In some ways, “ the amazing thing is not that these things occur, it’s that we notice them, ” according to David Spiegelhalter, a professor at the University of Cambridge who studies such things, as quoted in Julie Beck’s’ Atlantic article. You could say that being more attentive leads to registering more coincidences. Spiegelhalter, the article notes, has a website where people can submit their coincidence experiences, and claims to have collected something like 5,000 of them. The most common form is “ finding a link with someone you meet .” Obviously, this suggests that people who are looking for connections — who are open, curious, attentive to others — are more likely to find unexpected ones. “Coincidences never happen to me at all, because I never notice anything,” Spiegelhalter says (somewhat jokingly). “I never talk to anybody on trains. If I’m with a stranger, I don’t try to find a connection with them … .” I admit it never really occurred to me that there could be coincidence-friendly types . But Beck also cites another researcher who has found that certain personality traits are linked to experiencing more coincidences—people who describe themselves as religious or spiritual, people who are self-referential (or likely to relate information from the external world back to themselves), and people who are high in meaning-seeking are all coincidence-prone. The article goes on to explore everything from Jung’s idea of synchronicity to popular notions of the paranormal. Possibly the opposite of missing coincidences is reading too much meaning into mere chance occurrences that look like something more. The world shapes our attention, but sometimes attention shapes our world — for better or worse! That said, I’m attracted to this idea that “finding a link with someone you meet” is the most-reported form of coincidence. It’s a nice frame for chatting with someone new: Be curious, be open — and look for a happy coincidence or two. Leave a comment Thank you Suzanne! Noticing is about other people, too. title: The Personal Brand Trap: Why Humans Shouldn’t Think of Themselves as Brands
description: When I was a wee little boy growing up, I wanted to be a fireman. It seemed considerably more achievable than becoming a ThunderCat or Batman, which were my other career choices when I was eight. At school I had absolutely no clue what I wanted to do as a career. Potentially something arty or sporty, but back in the 90s I was told neither of those were money-makers, so I had to think about getting a proper job. Today, I would classify myself as a designer and educator helping the next generation of creatives build more opportunity for themselves. That feels very aligned with who I am today. But I have also been a barman, factory worker, waiter, tattoo apprentice, window cleaner, failed businessman, unemployable bum, and many other things on the journey to finding this particular version of me. And that is one of the wonderful things about being a human… nobody really freaking knows who they’re going to become. The person you are today is probably very different from the person you were five years ago, and if you’re doing this thing called life properly, there’s a good chance the person you’ll become five years from now will look different again. And, from what my mum tells me… that’s completely normal. Most of us are making it up as we go, collecting experiences and continuously falling forward into newer versions of ourselves… we’re supposed to evolve. So in this little article I want to share my perspective on a topic that I think deserves a little more questioning: personal branding. More specifically, I want to explore why I don’t think humans should think of themselves as brands, and why applying brand logic to a human being can potentially do more harm than good. Thanks for reading The Real Brand Life! Subscribe for free to receive new posts. Now, I’m not here to suggest that personal branding doesn’t exist. That would cause a riot. Instead, I’d like to challenge some of the advice being peddled around willy-nilly on the dopamine drug train that is social media. To do that, I think we first need to agree on the difference between brand logic and human logic. A brand’s job is to reduce complexity. Brands are trying to be recognised at scale and for that to happen, they need to simplify things. They need to make themselves easier to understand, remember and choose. They do that better when they are associated with a couple of very clear ideas. Humans, on the other hand, operate very differently my friends. We change our minds all the freaking time. We become interested in new things. We learn stuff, we grow our minds and then we see the world differently because of it. And an important thing to add is that humans don’t naturally operate at scale. We evolved in small communities and tribes, not in front of thousands of random people online. So if brands become stronger through consistency and humans become stronger through change, are we really sure those two things belong together? That’s why I find phrases like “you are your brand” and “everyone has a personal brand” a little, well… problematic. Being known for something and being a brand are not the same thing. I understand that these phrases are often being used as shortcuts, but even when I account for that nuance, I still think they fundamentally misunderstand what a brand is… and what a human needs. Now, I don’t want this to come across as a rant or a black-and-white argument, as some of the advice coming out of the personal brand camp is incredibly useful. Visibility matters for sure because if nobody knows what the heck you do, how on earth are they supposed to hire you? Other people need to know you exist people. I absolutely believe humans should become known. Known for doing good work, having interesting ideas, standing for something and making a positive impact on the people around them. But becoming known and becoming a product are not the same thing. Being known, or what most would simply call a reputation, is something people gift you over time. It forms through your behaviour and the way you consistently show up for yourself. You don’t have to manufacture it, force it or spend every waking minute trying to manage how you’re perceived by others. A reputation happens naturally as you continue growing into the person you’re becoming. And this is where I think we can run into trouble because the moment we start thinking of ourselves as a brand, our focus can shift. Instead of asking, “Who am I becoming?” we start asking, “How will this look to other people?” The danger is that we start viewing ourselves through the eyes of an audience before we’ve had chance to fully understand ourselves… we start looking at ourselves from the outside in. At first, that might not sound like too much of a problem. In fact, it actually sounds pretty bloody sensible. If you’re running a business, surely you should care about how people feel when they see you. But I don’t believe growth and perception always want the same thing. The thing about growth is that it can look a bit messy from the outside. You change your mind, let go of old ideas and, more often than we’d like to admit, realise you got something wrong. That’s all part of the process. And brand logic doesn’t particularly reward that kind of thinking. Brands gain strength through their consistency. They keep showing up in roughly the same way until people know exactly what to expect from them. And I think that’s where a lot of people can run into a bit of an issue. The more successful a personal brand becomes, the more pressure there can be to keep being the person your audience already knows. To keep talking about the same things, showing up in the same way and feeding the machine that made people pay attention in the first place. That’s the personal brand trap. The human becomes responsible for holding onto a version of themselves they may have already outgrown. And as we see more people choosing freelance careers, building solo businesses and creating opportunities for themselves online, I think this becomes an increasingly important conversation to navigate. I know that perception matters, visibility matters, being known matters, and creating opportunity matters… but so does growth as a human being. Perhaps the challenge isn’t figuring out how to turn people into brands… instead it’s figuring out how to help people become known without trapping them. I’d hate to think that personal branding, the very thing so many people turn to in search of more opportunity, could end up becoming the thing that stops them from becoming who they’re supposed to be. So if I can leave you with a little bit of advice here it would be this: focus on the things you want to be known for, but don’t lose sight of the person you’re becoming along the way. Maybe the goal isn’t to manage perception at all. Perhaps it’s simply to become someone worth paying attention to. Humans are supposed to evolve. Brands are supposed to repeat. The problems arise when we start applying the rules of one to the other, so don’t flatten yourself into a product mindset just because the internet tells you that’s the secret to success. Focus on becoming known for your craft, your kindness and your character. Keep sharing what matters to you because opportunity has a funny way of finding people who do. Just please remember to sprinkle a little patience on yourself along the way. Your mate, James Thoughts on this? Comment below team. I’m excited to hear what you think. title: Default Bias: Who chose your settings?
description: When a choice arrives with one option already set, most people leave it in place, regardless of whether it reflects their actual preference. The friction of changing something, combined with the implicit signal that the pre-set option is normal or recommended, produces consistent gravity toward the status quo. The mechanism runs through several channels at once. Loss aversion makes changing a default feel like risking something already owned. Implied endorsement suggests the default is a reasonable choice, so selecting it requires less justification. And the cognitive cost of evaluating alternatives encourages people to accept the existing state. These forces compound, especially in low-stakes or unfamiliar decisions where people lack strong preferences to override them. Default bias appears across organ donation programs, retirement savings enrollment, privacy settings, and software configuration. In each case, the same population of people produces dramatically different outcomes depending on which option requires action and which requires inaction. The default does not just simplify the interface. It determines the outcome for a large share of users. In design A user opens a new account and immediately lands in a signup flow. Before they have formed any preferences, the product has already decided: marketing emails are on, data sharing is enabled, notifications fire at full volume. The user clicks through, and the defaults stay. Default bias means the designer’s pre-set choices become most users’ permanent choices, whether or not those choices were made with the user’s benefit in mind. This places significant weight on the moment a default is chosen. Every pre-selected option is effectively a policy decision applied to the full user base. Designers who understand this use defaults to serve the majority, while keeping alternatives reachable. Those who ignore it discover that their defaults reflect internal convenience or business incentives rather than user needs. Applications in digital products Set the default communication preference to the least intrusive option, then let users escalate: email digests before individual notifications, not the reverse. When offering a free-to-paid upgrade, pre-select the plan that fits the user’s current usage, not the highest-tier plan, so the default reflects their situation. Place the destructive or irreversible action as the non-default: require an affirmative click to delete, unsubscribe, or share data, rather than treating those as pre-selected states. In onboarding forms, default empty fields to blank rather than placeholder values that users might submit without reading. On privacy and data settings, default to the most private configuration and present expansion as a deliberate user choice, not a correction of a setting they already “agreed to.” When a setting has a best-fit value for most users, pre-select it with a visible label like “Recommended” so the default carries transparent reasoning rather than hidden authority. Industry examples Countries with automatic organ donation enrollment see consent rates above 90%. Countries that require a positive registration act see rates below 20%. Same populations, different defaults. Thaler and Benartzi documented a similar pattern in 401(k) enrollment in 2003. Companies that switched retirement plans to automatic enrollment saw participation jump from around 50% to over 90%. Employees could still remove themselves. Most did not. Microsoft pre-selected telemetry and automatic update settings in Windows 10 that collected substantial user data. Changing them required navigating several menus. Few users did. Google enabled AI-assisted email completion in Gmail by default for all users. Adoption was high not because users chose it, but because disabling it required a deliberate action most skipped. Apple’s App Tracking Transparency, released in 2021, shifted ad tracking from an on-by-default state to an explicit prompt. Consent rates dropped from an estimated 70% to under 30%. No one changes what they don’t notice Changing a default requires two things most people avoid at the same time: forming a preference and acting on it. The pre-set option eliminates both requirements. People accept it without deliberating, often without noticing the choice was made. This is not a failure of attention, rather a rational response to cognitive load . When a decision is low-salience and the default seems reasonable, the cost of evaluating alternatives outweighs the benefit. The designer who sets the default has, in effect, already made the decision for the majority. This is why defaults carry ethical weight. A designer can claim to offer choice while structuring the choice so that most users never exercise it. Defaults are most powerful in one-time setup flows, where users move quickly and rarely return to revisit. Designers who want users to engage with settings should surface them at the moment of relevance, not bury them in preferences menus users open once and forget. Choosing the default is unavoidable. There is no neutral pre-selection. Every product that ships with a setting in place has already made a choice about whose interests that setting serves. Further reading The Power of Defaults — Jakob Nielsen, Nielsen Norman Group (2005) Defaults — The Decision Lab Status Quo Bias — The Decision Lab Choice Architecture 2.0: How People Interpret and Make Sense of Nudges — Job Krijnen, Behavioral Scientist (2018) Defaults Are Not the Same by Default — Jachimowicz, Duncan, Weber, and Johnson, Behavioral Scientist (2019) You just read why the pre-set option wins. So here’s one I’ve set for you: The reference designers keep open. Default Bias is 1 of 106 principles in Psychology of Design; the complete reference behind this newsletter. What attention does. How trust forms. Why habits stick. Each one written the way you just read this one: the mechanism, where it shows up, and how to use it. title: Karimoku New Standard and ASICS create furniture made from crushed trainers
description: Furniture brand Karimoku New Standard has announced the global release of its KNS x ASICS Collaboration, which repurposes upcycled foam from unused ASICS trainers as cushioning for two seating designs. The KNS x ASICS Collaboration uses deadstock and sample footwear from ASICS that would have otherwise been discarded. Karimoku New Standard, a sub-brand of Japanese manufacturer Karimoku , used the same technique that ASICS has utilised for its upcycled Neocurve trainers to create the material for the collaboration. ASICS trainers are crushed to extract EVA foam The ASICS footwear is dismantled, sorted and crushed to extract Ethylene Vinyl Acetate (EVA) foam, a flexible, light material commonly used as cushioning for midsoles, outsoles and footbeds. After the foam has been extracted, it is blended with cotton and paired with a three-millimetre condensed foam sheet to create a hybrid structure, according to Karimoku New Standard . The material is then used as cushioning in the brand's Castor Lobby Sofa and Polar Lounge Chair, which also feature an embroidered tag as a symbol of the collaboration. Read: Issey Miyake designs "minimalist" Hyper Taping trainers for ASICS The KNS x ASICS Collaboration, which was introduced in Japan earlier this year before the recent global launch, came about after Karimoku New Standard was working on seating for the meeting spaces in ASICS' Tokyo office. "Through rigorous sessions with ASICS – leveraging their expertise in sports science – and a meticulous adjustment process for real-world office use, Karimoku repeatedly prototyped to transform an unfamiliar material like shoe waste into true furniture comfort," Karimoku New Standard said. "This uncompromising, hands-on exploration led to the creation of the innovative hybrid structure," the brand continued. "Beyond merely reusing materials from a sustainability standpoint, it turns them into a functional added value." The Polar Lounge Chair was made using upcycled sneakers Karimoku has previously collaborated with brands including Zaha Hadid Design . ASICS recently released the "minimalist" Hyper Taping trainers with fashion brand Issey Miyake and has also designed pastel-coloured trainers with Danish brand Hay . title: Snøhetta completes landmark opera house in Shanghai
description: A giant spiral staircase guides visitors to the roof of the Shanghai Grand Opera House, which international studio Snøhetta designed to be "as much a civic destination as a performance venue". Located on the Huangpu River waterfront in Shanghai, China, the 146,786-square-metre opera house was conceived as a major cultural landmark that can accommodate a variety of musical performances. Snøhetta has completed the Shanghai Grand Opera House While Snøhetta 's design responds to a highly ambitious brief, the studio said it began the project as it always does, by taking time to examine and understand the specific site and its context, no matter the scale. According to the studio, this helped it to create the desired landmark while ensuring it felt like an extension of the existing public realm, open and accessible to both ticket holders and passersby. It is located on the Huangpu River waterfront "We always begin the same way, regardless of scale: by understanding the context," Snøhetta co-founder Kjetil Thorsen told Dezeen. "A cultural building, any building for that matter, must respond to its surroundings, the people who use it, the performers it serves, and the city it becomes part of," he reflected. "When I last visited the site, I was asked by a Chinese architecture student how we managed to create a building that felt so Chinese despite not being from China. The answer lies in observation and understanding context." Its key feature is a giant spiral staircase Shanghai Grand Opera House's defining feature is its spiral staircase, which dramatically cantilevers at its peak and was intended to emulate everything from an unfolding fan to a dancer or a set of piano keys. It leads directly to the publicly accessible rooftop, which doubles as a stage, an observation deck or simply a meeting point. According to Thorsen, it was integral to making the building feel part of the urban fabric. The staircase has a dramatic cantilever He compared the design to the Oslo Opera House , which the studio completed in 2000, with both designs actively seeking to "reduce thresholds wherever possible". "Buildings like opera houses inevitably create thresholds through walls, doors, and ticketed programs. We see it as our responsibility to challenge those thresholds and make the building as much a civic destination as a performance venue," Thorsen explained. "People should be able to enjoy the building without attending a performance. It should become part of everyday life, a place to spend time, meet others, and experience the city," he added. "A successful landmark is not only recognised by visitors, it is also embraced by the people who live around it and make it part of their everyday lives." The lobby is designed to feel light and open Shanghai Grand Opera House has a radial plan and contains a trio of auditoriums alongside exhibition and education spaces, restaurants and rehearsal and production areas. The facade flits between transparent and opaque finishes, depending on where the studio wanted to provide privacy and openness. For example, expansive glass elements maximise natural light and views in the lobby. The main auditorium has five levels Together, the three auditoriums can accommodate 4,200 people and host a range of performances. The main auditorium, called the Harmony Hall, contains 2,000 seats across its five levels, while the second hall, named the Soar Theatre, is more intimate, with space for 1,200 people. The final auditorium contains 1,000 seats and was constructed as a highly flexible space with adaptive seating and staging, catering to more experimental performances. It is fronted with a large glass facade overlooking the river. "For younger generations especially, that flexibility can help make cultural experiences feel more relevant, accessible, and connected to contemporary life," said Thorsen. Read: Snøhetta's Oslo Opera House was the most significant building of 2007 Shanghai Grand Opera House's material palette is a play of contrasts, with the light-coloured white stone, glass, and timber exterior having a more open feel than the darker, more intimate interiors. Inside, the auditoriums each have a unique aesthetic. The main hall is filled with deep red tones and surfaces, intended to feel as though they are carved from a single block, while lighter wooden materials characterise the other two. At night, the stage towers that project from the building are illuminated, shifting in colour to "animate the roof and the skyline". The smallest performance hall is designed to be adaptive Minimising the building's carbon footprint was a significant challenge due to the building's "scale and complexity", Thorsen said, but this was achieved through measures including passive design strategies. The bright roof reflects sunlight and heat rather than absorbing it, and the public lobby opens towards both the river and the park, allowing for cross-ventilation. A palette of durable materials and an adaptable interior will ensure a long lifespan for the building, while a close connection to public transport minimises dependence on private vehicles. Shanghai Grand Opera House is complete with a landscape design that connects to existing parkland, wetlands and public spaces to support local biodiversity and provide ample public space. The other auditorium accommodates 1,200 guests Snøhetta was founded by Thorsen and Craig Dykers in 1989. It won an international competition to design the opera house in 2016 and developed it with the state-owned firm East China Architectural Design & Research Institute (ECADI) and consultants Theatre Projects and Nagata Acoustics . Other major cultural projects by the studio include the Theodore Roosevelt Presidential Library in North Dakota and the rippled Glasshouse Theatre in Queensland . title: Baird Architects releases first furniture collection as "natural extension" of studio
description: US architecture studio Baird Architects has released its inaugural furniture collection, with seating, tables, and shelving, designed by in-house architects and collaborators and made in Portugal. The twelve-piece BA Objeto collection was led by Baird Architects founder Matthew Baird, who designed several pieces and also commissioned studio employees and collaborators. Each piece is credited to its designer, and the designers will receive a portion of the profits, according to Baird. Ines Gulbenkian designed an aluminium coffee table for the Ba Objeto collection The works include a solid walnut "surf" table by Baird, a swooping aluminium coffee table by Ines Gulbenkian and a dark brown cork bench by Gina Jiang. The pieces are primarily produced in Lisbon , Portugal, where Baird Architects has established a new studio to support its furniture making. Baird said a "considered approach to materiality, a crisp aesthetic, and a desire to push the boundaries of furniture design" draws the collection together. Gina Jiang created a cork made of a dark brown cork material The move points to an expansion of the studio's work beyond one-off furniture creation and illustrates a different business model for architecture studios. "Furniture feels like a natural extension of our architectural practice because it allows us to explore our interests in materiality, form, and craftsmanship at a more intimate scale," Baird told Dezeen. "We also wanted to create something that celebrates the individual designers within our studio, giving them the freedom to develop pieces of their own while contributing to a collective endeavour." Read: Apparatus draws on Persian mythology for its first full collection in five years Other pieces in the collection include a mirror by Portuguese designer Teresa Mascarenhas and a plywood and leather chair by designer Katy Cheng. Baird said the collection is an extension of the furniture the studio has created for private clients over the years, and that the team is already "looking ahead" to a second collection. Baird Architects commissioned Portuguese architect Teresa Mascarenha for the project From design fairs to heritage brands, designers and architects are currently attempting to restructure business models in the design world, primarily to receive more profit and credit for their work. title: Spaces by Manah signposts Chennai community centre with barrel-vaulted roof
description: Local architecture studio Spaces by Manah has completed The Soil & Sea community centre in Chennai, India , with a brick barrel-vaulted roof that serves as a "visible landmark" on the site. The 4,330-square-metre building was designed to provide learning space for a local education centre, as well as to house community workshops and events. Spaces by Manah designed its single-storey masonry structure to appear as though it were "growing out of the existing landscape", creating a series of outdoor and open-air spaces that overlook its lush surroundings. Spaces by Manah has completed a community centre in Chennai, India "The project sits within a lush, tree-lined parcel of land with the design growing out of the existing landscape," the studio told Dezeen. "The building is positioned to retain its connection with the trees and outdoor spaces through a sequence of shaded, open and enclosed spaces, while the dominant barrel vault rises above the canopy to create a visible landmark within the site," it added. Raised on a rubble stone foundation, the centre is organised around a flat-roofed volume, flanked on two sides by an L-shaped verandah that was conceived by the studio as an "intermediate, informal zone" between the building and landscape. A barrel-vaulted roof crowns the gathering space Steps and a ramp at the building's front lead up to the verandah, which is sheltered by the barrel-vaulted roof on one side to form a main gathering space for the community. Meanwhile, its other edge is topped with a sloping, tiled roof. A series of granite stone pillars frame the space, along with built-in seating. Read: Sculptural music centre shows bamboo as "a serious construction material" "The architecture responds to this idea through a strong central gathering space, expressed by the barrel vault, with more intimate and informal spaces arranged around it," the studio said. "An L-shaped veranda acts as an intermediate, informal zone between the enclosed spaces and the landscape, with built-in seating and ramps supporting movement, accessibility and interaction throughout the building." Granite stone pillars and Mangalore tiles complement the building's brick walls The bricks used for the structure's load-bearing walls were left exposed throughout the space. To complement the brick design, the studio sourced doors, windows and Mangalore floor tiles locally and repurposed them throughout the building. This materiality extends to the building's interior, where exposed brick walls and roof elements are set off by glossy tiles. "The material palette was intentionally kept natural, tactile and largely raw, allowing the building to sit comfortably within its landscape," the studio said. Glossy tiles are used within the interior Also on the site is a separate toilet block, which is similarly perched atop a stone foundation, and complete with load-bearing brick walls and a tiled canopy roof. Elsewhere in Chennai, Ekarth Studio has used bamboo to form a sculptural venue for the Maestro Ilaiyaraaja Centre for Music Learning and Research , while Habitat Collaborative has threaded a curved school through a tree-filled site in Vadodara .
