title: Factory in Bangladesh that "redefines manufacturing architecture" wins RIBA International Prize
description: A rug factory in Rangpur, Bangladesh , designed by Dhaka-based studio Nakshabid Architects to dismantle workplace hierarchies, has won the RIBA International Prize for 2026. Named Green Field Factory, the project is the fifth winner of the biennial award, presented by the Royal Institute of British Architects (RIBA) to the world's best new building outside the UK. Nakshabid Architects was praised by the RIBA jury for designing a factory that incorporates passive design principles and prioritises the wellbeing of its 5,000 employees. Green Field Factory won this year's RIBA International Prize. Photo by City Syntax "Green Field Factory redefines manufacturing architecture in South Asia and beyond," said RIBA president Chris Williamson. "By putting people, wellbeing and their everyday experiences at its core and actively supporting its female workforce, it proves that thoughtful design can dismantle traditional hierarchies to create profound social and environmental change." It was announced as the RIBA International Prize winner at the Stirling Prize ceremony in London last night. This year's prestigious Stirling Prize was given to Mary Duggan Architects and Ruff Architects for the Lion Green Road housing development in London. The factory has a monumental green wall. Photo by City Syntax Commissioned by rug manufacturer Karupannya Rangpur Limited , Green Field Factory is a seven-storey building surrounded by fields and small settlements. Nakshabid Architects based the design on the traditional Bengali home, incorporating natural ventilation and biophilic design principles. Courtyards, verandas, gardens and a monumental green facade were designed to let natural light and airflow into the building, minimising the need for mechanical systems. Nakshabid Architects designed the building with passive ventilation. Photo by Prantography Green Field Factory has one main entrance with two grand staircases for all workers, intended to challenge hierarchies in the workplace. This responds to other factories in the area that have separate entrances for factory workers and people in management roles. Shared spaces in the factory provide areas for workers to take breaks and socialise. Other areas are designated to support workers' families and the wider community during the day and outside of working hours, including a rooftop daycare centre, on-site medical practice, grocery shop and prayer room. A connection to nature is provided through low-maintenance planting throughout, which also supports insects and birds, while artwork and sculptures celebrate the role of women in the workplace, family and community. Read: "Welcoming and inclusive" London housing wins RIBA Stirling Prize 2026 "The project demonstrates the dissolution of architecture as a topological space, with a single-pointed focus on dismantling civilisational oppression and hierarchy, for woman and man alike," said grand jury chair Bijoy Jain. "Through the simple gesture of two grand stairs as an equanimous shared portal, it transforms a space and symbol once reserved exclusively for the king of the region, as landlord and ruling class, and for the colonial power that pervaded the length and breadth of the country," he continued. "The architect and owner shared how the women and men working in the factory would bring their families with pride to show them where they worked, and the women empowered in their self-reliance to take life and familial decisions on their own." The jury praised the design for prioritising the wellbeing of the factory employees. Photo by Karupannya Rangpur The RIBA International Prize is awarded biennially to a building that "demonstrates visionary, innovative thinking, and design excellence whilst making a distinct contribution for its users and within its physical context". Green Field Factory was selected ahead of BRAC University in Bangladesh by WOHA, Z33 art museum in Belgium by Francesca Torzo Architetto and the renovation of Royale Belge in Belgium by Caruso St John Architects, Bovenbouw Architectuur and DDS+. YIMBY by Maker Architecten was named the winner of the International Emerging Architect Award. Photo by Stijn Bollaert Alongside the International Prize, RIBA awarded this year's International Emerging Architect Award to Maker Architecten for its YIMBY residential project in Kortrijk, Belgium. The project revamped 18 plots across a 1920's garden city neighbourhood, utilising reclaimed materials for new facades and creating communal green space. In 2024, Peris + Toral Arquitectes won the RIBA International Prize for an "inclusive and sustainable" social housing project in Barcelona. The top photo is by Mud Canvas. title: What is "the gravity of average" and why is it holding you back?
description: I grew up believing one thing: Don’t be average. Looking back now, as an older, slightly fatter man, there’s something wonderfully ironic about that particular piece of advice. While every person in authority was telling me not to become average, the systems around me were teaching me exactly how to become it. School teaches us there was one right answer. Business teaches us there’s a right process. Algorithms tell us there’s a right format. Most industries have their own best practices, and society at large constantly reminds us that fitting in is safer than standing out. None of these proven systems are bad. In fact, they’re incredibly useful. They help us educate millions of little people, build reliable businesses, and make sense of an increasingly complicated world. But when you start stacking them on top of one another, year after year, decade after decade… something intriguing happens. They all pull us in the exact same direction: Toward what’s proven Toward what’s predictable Toward what’s familiar Toward the flipping middle We hear a lot these days about falling test scores, declining creativity, and a lack of ambition. I’m not convinced that’s the whole story. I think we’re living inside an ecosystem of invisible forces that constantly reward the safest path. Millions of perfectly sensible decisions, made by perfectly sensible people, combine to suck us toward the same ideas until we all end up in the exact same place… the fookin’ middle. I call this: the gravity of average. Whether we realize it or not, we’ve been caught in its invisible pull since the day we were born… damn it. Here are the five layers of gravity conspiring against us all, and why you need to fight them with everything you’ve got to protect your individual magic. 1. Educational gravity Our first experience of this gravity starts in the classroom. School has an incredibly difficult job: educating millions of children fairly and consistently, often with limited resources and enormous expectations. The only way to make that possible is to rely on standardized curricula, rigid grading schemes, and easily measured outcomes. From a very young age, we learn to optimize for what gets rewarded … the gold stars, the praise from teachers, the good-old pats on the back. Before long, we’re no longer just learning the subject, we’re learning how to succeed within the system. The educational environment doesn’t intentionally produce average people. Far from it. But when success is measured in the exact same way for everyone, it’s only natural that millions of children begin chasing the exact same things. The more people optimize for the identical outcome, the more they will eventually look alike… it’s the logical outcome of a predictable system. 2. Economic gravity Businesses only exist if they survive, and to do that, they have to make rational decisions. If a pricing model has worked before, why change it? If a marketing strategy has proven successful, why reinvent it? If a competitor is growing using a particular approach, it’s only natural to copy it. None of these are bad decisions. Economist Harold Hotelling described this exact phenomenon in what became known as Hotelling’s Law . When businesses compete for the same customers, they naturally drift toward one another rather than away. Differentiation feels risky, while similarity feels sensible. Over time, this way of thinking compounds. What starts as “best practice” gradually becomes the default way of doing business. When an entire industry chases the identical measures of success (revenue, profit, or market share), even the most original business ideas eventually drift toward the average when they optimize for the same thing. 3. Social gravity As humans, we’ve always worried about belonging. For most of human history, being accepted by the group dramatically increased our chances of not becoming dead. That instinct is still hardwired into us. One of my favourite psychology experiments that backs this up comes from Solomon Asch . Participants were invited into a room to complete what they thought was a simple test about the length of a few lines. What they didn’t know was that everyone else in the room was an actor hired to be in on the experiment. The answers were obvious, but one by one, the actors deliberately gave the wrong answer. Faced with an entire room disagreeing with them, many participants ignored what they could clearly see and went along with the crowd instead. Around 75% of people conformed at least once, even though the group was clearly wrong. Nobody has to tell us to fit in. We just learn which parts of ourselves earn acceptance and which parts are safer left hidden. 4. Algorithmic gravity Welcome to the newest kid on the block. Algorithms don’t care about “silly” things like originality… all they give a poop about is retention. The easiest way to predict what will keep your attention is to look at what has already worked. Successful ideas become recommendations. Recommendations become trends. Trends become the templates that every influencer and their dog starts copying. Before long, thousands of people are creating different versions of the exact same thing because that’s what the system keeps serving up. Social media isn’t in the business of finding the next brilliant idea. It’s in the business of keeping us scrolling, and scrolling, and scrolling. And the easiest way to do that is by feeding us a slightly repackaged version of the average… the baseline of everything the system has already gobbled up before. 5. Professional gravity Every profession develops its own “playbook.” Designers have processes, marketers have foolproof plans, and consultants have their frameworks. Most of these defaults exist because someone, at some point, solved a real problem for a real person… hurrah. The danger happens when best practice subtly becomes the only practice. The longer an approach survives unquestioned, the more it feels like common sense. Before long, entire industries are repeating formulas that worked 30 years ago, even though the world has completely evolved around them. The comfort zone is a very dangerous place. Nothing grows there, as they say. The optimization trap What I’ve realized about these five forces is that they all share the exact same mischievous mechanism. Every system must decide what success looks like and, once it does, the rest of us naturally optimize for it. School rewards grades. Business rewards revenue. Algorithms reward engagement. Society rewards acceptance. Professions reward best practice. None of the above are bad… but when millions of people chase the exact same measures of success, gravity takes over. Human beings are remarkably good at adapting to their environment. The more we align ourselves with the same definition of success, the more we begin to resemble one another. And today, more people than ever are finding themselves in the middle. For most of history, becoming competent at something took years of deliberate practice. Today, technology can get almost anyone to “good enough” in a matter of minutes. Technology is closing the gap from below, while optimization is closing the gap from above. People who once struggled to produce competent work can now create something perfectly passable with better tools. At the same time, many of the people who were once exceptional are handing more of their thinking over to those same tools. In the pursuit of speed they often sacrifice the originality and personality that made them stand out in the first place. One force lifts people into the middle. The other pulls people back towards it. Now, there is absolutely nothing wrong with being average. Millions of people build fulfilling careers, do meaningful work, and live brilliant lives without ever trying to stand out. But commercially, today, average is becoming a far riskier place to build a future. To riff on something Rory Sutherland once said: when you become logical, you become predictable. And when you become predictable, you become replaceable. That doesn’t mean you should reject logic or stop using new technology. It simply means those things are no longer enough. They help you meet the standard, yes, but they’ll never make you the obvious choice. I’ve come to believe that opportunity doesn’t flow toward the middle. It flows toward recognizable differences that people trust. The gravity of average never disappears. You simply decide whether to drift with it… or spend your time pushing against it. Maybe that’s what Mr. Hotelling was trying to tell us all along. Test the edges. - James This article first appeared in my Fast Company column. You can check it out here .

title: Thin concrete plane defines minimalist villa in Ibiza by Fran Silvestre Arquitectos
description: A thin white-concrete plane folds and steps down a hillside to enclose Bellavista 11, a minimalist home overlooking the sea in Ibiza , designed by Spanish studio Fran Silvestre Arquitectos . Bellavista 11 is the first villa to be completed in The Roca Views development, a cluster of six homes designed by the Valencia-based studio in the town of Roca Lisa on Ibiza's eastern coast. The villas will be united by pared-back, rectilinear forms with thin white walls, designed by Fran Silvestre Arquitectos as a contemporary take on the island's traditional white-walled buildings. Fran Silvestre Arquitectos has completed a minimalist white villa in Ibiza "The project begins with a very simple question, 'Can we build on this hillside by placing a single element on it?'," studio founder Fran Silvestre told Dezeen. "The aim is to create a continuous element that follows the topography and, through its different folds, gradually finds the best conditions offered by the site," he explained. "It is an apparently very simple operation that allows many things to be resolved at once – adapting to the slope, organising the programme, orienting each room towards a different condition of the landscape and extending the architecture to generate shade." The home is framed by a thin concrete plane Bellavista 11 is divided across three low-slung volumes, beginning at the top with a garage and access stair, moving through to a central social volume and ending in a block of five bedrooms. The thin white concrete plane that defines the home is just 15 centimetres thick. As it steps down the site, it creates expansive roof terraces atop the lowest two volumes, folding around to create the interior floor plates and a series of lower terraces. Read: Fran Silvestre Arquitectos creates walkway on top of glazed Hoffman House "We like to think in terms of an evolved tradition, learning from what works in Mediterranean architecture – shade, protection from the sun, clarity of materials – and resolving it through contemporary construction techniques," said Silvestre. Alongside the open-plan living, dining and kitchen space is a swimming pool, while the bedroom block overlooks a seating terrace. Both are accessed via walls of full-height sliding glass doors with slender frames and hidden tracks. It features a terrace with a pool The villa's interiors continue the deliberate simplicity of the exterior, with white walls, pale stone floors and timber carpentry chosen to emphasise the movement of light and shadow across surfaces throughout the day. "White appears naturally because of its relationship with traditional Mediterranean architecture and because of its performance under intense solar radiation," Silvestre explained. "At the same time, it allows light to transform the spaces throughout the day. This is something that particularly interests us, we understand light almost as another material within the project." Minimalist finishes feature throughout the project Silvestre founded his eponymous practice in 2005. The studio previously used a similarly singular geometric gesture for a home in Madrid, which is housed in a cluster of white cylindrical volumes . Its other recent projects include the stepped Villa 95 in Andalusia and the winding Sabater House in Alicante . The photography is by Jesus Orrico . title: Eight converted power stations that show the power of reuse
description: In this roundup , we take a look at decommissioned power stations that have been given a second life , from the Tate Modern museum in London to the Dyson headquarters in Singapore. Originally built to generate electricity, these industrial buildings typically have expansive interiors with tall ceilings, giving architects plenty of flexibility for conversion. Photo by Hufton & Crow Battersea Power Station, UK, by WilkinsonEyre The Grade II*-listed Battersea Power Station in London stood decommissioned for 39 years before architecture studio WilkinsonEyre 's transformation reopened it as a shopping, office and residential building in 2022. Originally built in the 1930s, a bustling shopping centre is now located in the building's restored turbine halls and glazed apartments were built atop the roof. Find out more about Battersea Power Station › Photo by Peter Sherno Ballers, USA, by Good City Studio and Hexagon Studio Architects Local firms Good City Studio and Hexagon Studio Architects revamped the main turbine hall of Delaware Power Station in Fishtown, Philadelphia , into a sports club with indoor pickleball, soccer and squash courts. Named Ballers, the sports club formed part of the wider plan to transform the 1920s power station into The Battery, a mixed-use complex containing apartments, offices and a hotel. Find out more about Ballers › Photo courtesy of Dyson Dyson headquarters, Singapore, by M Moser Associates, W Architects and Studio Lapis Technology company Dyson established its global company headquarters inside Singapore 's St James Power Station, which was transformed by local studios W Architects and Studio Lapis, with interior fit-out by architecture studio M Moser Associates. The turbine hall of the 1926 building was reimagined as a four-storey atrium framed by exposed black steelwork and a sculptural spiral staircase , while an area of amphitheatre-style seating provides gathering space next to a cafe. Find out more about the Dyson headquarters › Photo by Margherita Spiluttini Tate Modern, UK, by Herzog & de Meuron Iconic London landmark the Tate Modern was once the Bankside Power Station, originally designed by Giles Gilbert Scott, who also designed Battersea Power Station. Swiss studio Herzog & de Meuron 's pioneering transformation of the building opened in 2000, complete with a cathedral-like gallery space in the turbine hall, and ignited a global trend of converting disused power stations into hubs of art and culture. Find out more about Tate Modern › Photo by Iwan Baan Powerhouse Arts, USA, by Herzog & de Meuron In more recent years, Herzog & de Meuron converted the remains of a 115-year-old power plant in Brooklyn into an art manufacturing hub called Powerhouse Arts. The studio refurbished the brick-clad turbine hall, the only part of the original building left standing, and converted it into an art production centre, while the demolished Boiler House was rebuilt in red concrete . Find out more about Powerhouse Arts › Photo by Bai Yu Shajing Village Hall, China, by ARCity Office As part of wider plans to transform an industrial site into a public wetland, architecture studio ARCity Office restored and extended a 1980s power plant in Shenzhen , China, converting it into a community hub . The studio left the building's concrete remnants as-found, using its structural shell to support a series of new steel and glass volumes that draw upon the spaces found in traditional ancestral halls. Find out more about Shajing Village Hall › Photo by Hufton + Crow. Global Leadership Centre, UK, by John McAslan + Partners British studio John McAslan + Partners added learning space and accommodation to Oxford's first electrical power plant to form the Global Leadership Centre, designed for the University of Oxford 's Saïd Business School. John McAslan + Partners created a triple-height entrance and shared space in the turbine hall, restored the 1890s brick facades and rebuilt and extended the metal-clad upper levels. Find out more about Global Leadership Centre › Photo by Tycho Merijn Innovation Powerhouse, the Netherlands, by Atelier van Berlo, Eugelink Architectuur and De Bever Architecten The former Philips power plant in Eindhoven was converted into an innovation hub housing a dozen businesses, with offices arranged along a communal street-like passage. Rotterdam-based Atelier van Berlo worked with Eindhoven-based studios Eugelink Architectuur and De Bever Architecten on the project, aiming to celebrate the building's original features by preserving its structure and coal chutes. description: Welcome to the latest edition of OBJECTS QUARTERLY, a roundup of object-related items of interest published, uh, quarterly, for supporters of The Art of Noticing. Attending to objects is a sub-theme of TAoN, and a favorite subject of mine. Revisit prior OQ issues, and other mindful materialism posts, here . Enjoy ! Via Wikipedia . By Arpingstone - Arpingstone, Public Domain, https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?curid=38786 “KIM’S GAME” Today I have another object-centric attention game borrowed from fiction — borrowed twice over, in fact. It comes from a short story callled “ Kim’s Game, ” by Sadia Shepard, published in The New Yorker earlier this year. In the story, a character recalls a childhood game that his father evidently took from Rudyard Kipling’s Kim : “My father would arrange a handful of objects on a tray—an old coin, a ribbon, a rock, a thimble, that sort of thing—and ask me to memorize them. Then he’d cover the tray with a newspaper and ask me to describe what I remembered. Sometimes, he’d take something away to see if I noticed . In the Kipling novel, the game is part of Kim’s training to be a spy.” This turns out to have become a well-known game , played (with variations) by children, the Cub Scouts , the military, and others. It actually sounds like a fun exercise — and also potentially a great assignment, particularly for a writing class. (And for the record it does sound like decent spy training, too.) If you try it, or have played it in the past, tell me about it! And as always I welcome your object-centered attention games, from fiction or real life. description: * Reminder: The Savor of the Month theme for October is WATER. Details here ; Supporters can share their findings in the thread here . Check it out! Back in August, I tried a little experiment: publishing a question from my ongoing Icebreaker series as a stand-alone post, rather than a secondary item in the main newsletter. The hope was that this would encourage readers to actually answer in the comments. And it did! So I’m doing it again. All are welcome to chime in. Noticing is about other people, too. The Icebreaker series aims to help with that. There’s a central collection spot for all the icebreakers to date, here . Today’s icebreaker comes from me. What is the most recent, or most personally important, book that you’ve read twice (or more)? I would probably stipulate no children’s books; I think that’s a different discussion. But otherwise I’d be open to just seeing where the question leads — I think it’s somehow more interesting than just asking for someone’s “favorite” book. This subject of re-reading books has popped up randomly a couple of times for me lately, and made me think about how long it’s been since I’ve done it. I guess I now worry that I just don’t have enough time to repeat a book when there are so many I haven’t read once! That said, the most recent was The Ladies’ Paradise , by Zola, which I read for a second time about 10 years ago. The book I’ve read the most times is Native Son , three times (all in my 20s, I believe). What about you? Love to hear your thoughts! Leave a comment And please send your favorite icebreaker (whether you made it up or found it elsewhere) to consumed@robwalker.net . Previously: OKAY THAT’S IT! As always, I value your feedback (suggestions, critiques, positive reinforcement, constructive insults directed at me, not at anyone else , etc.), as well as your tips or stories or personal noticing rituals, things we need a word for, and of course your icebreakers : consumed@robwalker.net. Or use the comments. —> Or just click the heart symbol. That always makes my day. Pics via SignedPG Hi all, I was thinking about saving this for the next Objects Quarterly , but it deserves its own post. Here’s the story. A few weeks ago I shared an icebreaker question suggested by valued reader Judi K: “What is something you decided not to spend money on — that you now wish you had?” Among the dozens of great answers was a little tale from SignedPG about his rather charming interest in the Big Boy restaurant chain, and his resulting collection of Big Boy items involving its amusing mascot/logo character . This sparked a bit of a sub-thread about Big Boy, but that’s another matter. For today’s purposes, here’s the key passage from SignedPG: During a road trip my partner and I went into this huge antique/vintage store, and right in the front was this Big Boy plastic figurine. It was $40, maybe the size of a Coke bottle, and I wanted it badly. The problem was that in the moment I convinced myself that my collection was stupid. I saw my reflection in the glass display, and I was just mean to myself.
